title: reflecting on labyrinth, season 1
content:
season 2 of Labyrinth will run Feb 16 - May 16, 2026

explore labyrinth

labyrinth library is a community seasonal container I created last fall, for and with its first season of 24 community members. the central theme at its heart is — how to navigate the spiraling, nonlinear journey of the unknown — in your life, work, and creative practice.

I wrote about how I intially had the idea for labyrinth, here — and how the idea emerged from my desire to offer an ongoing community structure — a form with rhythm and depth, something which holds my body of teachings on process — which only deepens in richness and substance, over time.

if this website is the public garden-world of my body of work, then labyrinth is the secret, gated garden path, connected to a library. it is a walking path, and an intimate study room — where we deepen in our practices, in community, with my guidance.

today, as I’m slowly simmering on how I want to build the next season, I want to reflect on each element of labyrinth, and share reflections on how it felt.

ELEMENTS OF LABYRINTH, SEASON 1

overall experience
weekly discussions
whatsapp group chat
artifacts
personal journals
treks
show & tells
workshops

overall experience

overall, season 1 of Labyrinth far exceeded my expectations, and I was thrilled. I was nervous about starting an ongoing community container — especially as a facilitator who needs space and time to disappear. Labyrinth did for me what it did for many of its members — it gave me a latticework pattern; a flexible, supportive structure that kept me accountable — to my practice, to the work itself, and to the community. even on my worst of days, showing up for Labyrinth felt nourishing to my soul.

the community

for me, and for many of its members, what made Labyrinth most special were the community members.

I don’t know that I can do justice in describing them, but the overarching qualities that stood out at me, as a group, are — deep feeling, sensitive, artistic, spiritual, thoughtful, heart-full and generous, empathetic, often times high functioning / recovering from conventional, linear models of success, and yet, idiosyncratic and courageous enough to keep doing their own thing, to find their own way. there are many artists, many with their own businesses, many in search of integration between the different parts of themselves.

they ask important questions, they take responsibility for their growth, and they share the journey with each other — without any air of performativity. there is a humility, vulnerability, and strength to them. I was so grateful and inspired. and, honestly — I was relieved. because 12 weeks is a long time to spend with people you feel just okay about. but I loved and felt deep care for them, and felt their love and care for each other.

that was my sense of the emotional tone of Labyrinth: a community of open, honest, vulnerable, grounded, creative, empathetic people, who show up for themselves, and for each other.

12 week seasonal / weekly rhythm

I know that many community/membership models are monthly or annual — active until you cancel. but, I don’t even know that I can commit to that indefinite, open-ended nature, let alone ask my members to commit. I wanted the container of an entire season (12 weeks, or 3 months) — which I measured in 3 astrological signs.

12 weeks feels like long enough time for real change to happen — long enough to notice reoccuring patterns, for people to dip in and out, and to be flexible with whatever was happening in their lives. it meant members could disappear and return when they felt ready, and to find comfort in being able to reengage with Labyrinth as a community portal — to help them reconnect with their own creative practice.

my intention is that there is a minimum of ~1 month break between each season of Labyrinth.

a nonlinear, infinite feast

apart from the community containers, I created a significant amount of material for Labyrinth. in season 1, there were 12 artifacts and 3 workshops.

the reason for this is because I wanted Labyrinth to still exist, outside of the live community containers. I wanted quiet study rooms of a mystery library. I wanted it feel nourishing for people who preferred to be in a more receptive, hermit phase; who couldn’t make it to meetings, or wanted to engage with the teachings on their own. sometimes, I feel that way, so I wanted to give members an option.

but, as I repeated again and again — there was no way to fall “behind” in Labyrinth. not every teaching would be relevant to where you were, in that moment of your journey. but it would be available to you, indefinitely — like an infinite feast that you could return to, whenever you needed some nourishment.

  

weekly 90 min discussions

the ongoing live touchpoint for Labyrinth were its weekly discussion sessions — which were 90 minutes, drop-in. because we had 24 members across 8 time zones, some weeks, I tried to schedule 2 sessions for Europe/Australia time. most of our discussion sessions were between 5-8 people, which felt like an intimate size to have meaningful, meaty discussions.

we experimented with 3 types of discussion sessions

  • open discussion — I welcomed anyone to bring their questions or thoughts, and we explored them together

  • show & tells — where a community member would sign up to talk about their process and work for 20 min, and we’d organically branch off to related topics

  • themed discussion — we did a deep dive around exploring a specific topic (ie, “abundance is a feast”)


each session had audio recordings + transcripts — for anyone who couldn’t make it to listen, afterwards.

I know that many members got so much out of our discussion sessions — it helped them feel seen, witnessed, supported, and resourced by the group — in whatever they were grappling with.

 
 

whatsapp group chat + email


we had a WhatsApp group chat — which I used as a channel to send reminders and links to all the resources/teachings I created for Labyrinth, as well as polls for workshop or discussion topics.

I also sent a brief weekly email digest on Mondays.

the group chat was also crucial in that it gave members a space to share their reflections, questions, or thoughts in a more asynchronous, intimate space. I loved listening to voice messages, responding to them — and listening to community responses.

when community members had something they wanted to celebrate or share, they’d drop it into the chat. I count a community a success when it feels as though people are supporting each other, in a intertwining web.

 


artifacts

artifacts are metaphorical-practical tools for the journey of navigating the unknown. each artifact is a 10-20 minute audio recording, which included:

  • the metaphorical tool

  • a core guiding question to explore

  • unpacking the nuance, questions, challenges

  • invitation and practices to work with this artifact

the artifacts are themed by each astrological season, so this first season, we had artifacts for Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius. I explored these themes in this podcast episode:

the twelve artifacts of season 1 were

  1. The Compass

  2. The Sword

  3. The Glacier

  4. Storm Shelter

  5. Zombie Tunnel

  6. Dead End

  7. Torture Chamber

  8. Haunted House

  9. Bow & Arrow

  10. Feast Table

  11. Signal Fire

  12. Cliff Edge

 
 

personal journals + notion ecosystem


everything in Labyrinth was hosted in a Notion dashboard — which felt like its own rabbit-holey, nonlinear exploration play space. (I use Notion for all of my courses, and pretty much exclusively as my digital planning / process repository.)

inside the Notion dashboard, each member had their own personal journal space — which they could inhabit however they wanted.

community members used their personal journals to explore Labyrinth materials, think through process outloud, talk about their work, or share threads with each other. the journals were an asynchronous space for people to engage more deeply with witnessing each others’ process, and their own. journals occupied this liminal space between public/private — space to explore, space to be witnessed, space to connect — but without pressure.

  

creative treks

treks are 1 or 2 week, structured creative practice periods — where we go on a “group hike” together — each walking to our individual destinations. we did three treks during one season of Labyrinth. in a trek, each community member choses what they want to work on:

  • an existing project — or a new project

  • a creative practice

  • a sharing practice

  • walking, meditating, resting, anything

in a trek, there’s daily accountability, shared comradarie, and community around our individual projects/practices. to structure a trek, I’ll ask everyone to share their intentions, define tiny containers, and complete a daily trekking log, which I (and many community members) would check on daily and leave comments. I emphasized flexibility in trekking — not the tyranny of the daily streak, but welcoming participants to drop in and out, or change their treks, mid-way.

we then gathered for discussion sessions to explore what we learned, and discovered.

the treks felt deeply fulfilling — they worked. I think people felt that the tether of community helped them stay more present with their practice and process, and thus, accountable. I certainly felt that way.

 

show & tells

show & tells are when community members sign-up to speak for 20 minutes on their process, ongoing projects, a specific theme, or their work overall. we then have a discussion about it afterwards.

in season 1, six community members gave show & tells — about their various creative obsessions, ongoing practices, their websites, and multi-faceted bodies of work.

shea shared the organic evolution of their art practice
Shenee shared her branding work on core themes
Nina shared her digital home, travel projects, & spiritual foundations
Woz shared her body of work through her website
Alex shared his process of building a website + studio notes
LJ shared their communal writing practice, atmospheres.


they were all amazing! show & tells were such a beautiful way for each community member to gather, integrate, and talk about their work — and be witnessed and supported in the process. each show & tell felt like a two-way giving and recieving — less like a “talk” and more like a gathering of creative friends.

(this is why I named it such an elementary-esque name — to take off the pressure to have anything polished, to encourage you to stand up and just open your mouth — and see what comes out. Labyrinth is a safe space for that).

  

workshops

I created three workshops for this season of Labyrinth —

  • Labyrinth as a Map for Wayfinding — about using the structure/metaphor of labyrinth to set intentions for the season

  • Playgrounds & Cocoons — on shaping containers to hold creative energy

  • Embodied Abundance — cultivating the feeling of more than enough

the first was a 20 min introductory workshop, and the last two were both ~2 hour workshops that I taught live.

I’ve been wanting to create standalone workshops for a very long time, but get so wrapped up in teaching my longer courses. plus, it takes me significant energy to meet and engage with new people in live workshops. Labyrinth was my experimental playground for taking a concept and making a workshop teaching out of it, to serve my existing community.

the process was this:

  • I listened to the themes that emerged during our conversations

  • I came up with 3 workshop ideas, and sent a poll to the community.

  • I commited to one idea — disappeared for 4-5 days to make the workshop.

  • I delivered it live.


most likely, I will be releasing these workshops as standalone offerings after each season of Labyrinth.

  

 

misc. spaces

the elements I wrote about above formed the main essence of Labyrinth. however, I also created miscellaneous other spaces — inside the Notion ecosystem, as side experiments. including:

Conversation Threads — a “forum” of sorts, where community members can ask questions and respond to them, asynchronously, on their own time, without it getting buried in a feed. threads were organized by topics.

Inspiration Logs — where people can share works that inspired them — links, resources, books, podcasts, etc.

“Wild” Tab — a “process notebook” page in notion where I dropped in things I was working on, experiments, ideas, unreleased podcast episodes, random things. it’s like something in between my private Notion journals + my public website.

it was a messy and spontaneous documentation of my creative process — stuff that may or may not make it to my website, eventually.

 

closing notes


what I most loved about my experience of creating Labyrinth — apart from the magic and heart of its community members — was that it represented a delicate balance between a consistent, rhythmic structure — and an organic, spontaneous flow.

  • WEEKLY — discussion sessions + artifacts

  • MONTHLY — treks + workshops

  • ONGOING — chat, journals, notion spaces, show & tell


I had no idea what the artifacts would be, until I created them. I had no idea how the workshops would unfold, until I outlined them. I had no idea what people would share in their show & tells, until they happened.

it was a prime example of something I’ve worked my entire career to feel — that structure + spontaneity were perfectly in balance. it had enough structure to feel safe, grounded, earthy, AND enough possibility to feel alive, inspired, juicy.

this dance like an absolute necessity in navigating the labyrinthian paths of the creative life. it must feel safe — and it must feel free to change. otherwise I would not keep doing it. this is what keeps me walking.

the second season of Labyrinth will run: February 16 - May 17 2026
